texto: At about ten past seven on a November night, a voice on the radio said five calm words.
We are holding our own.
Minutes later, the ship they came from was gone. Seven hundred and twenty-nine feet of steel, off the radar.
No mayday. No distress call. Twenty-nine men on board, and not one of them was ever found.
For fifty-one years, the Coast Guard, the safety board, the shipping industry and the divers have argued about what happened in those few minutes.
Four theories. None proven.
Brother Quill here. Let's open the book.
The Edmund Fitzgerald went into the water on June seventh, 1958. She was the biggest ship on the Great Lakes.
Her crews called her the Mighty Fitz. She made about seven hundred and forty-eight round trips.
And she kept setting cargo records, because on the lakes, a ship is a machine for moving as much iron as possible.
But more iron means less ship. According to one recent book, welds instead of rivets saved her about one point two million pounds, and every pound saved was a pound of cargo.
Then the rules changed in her favor. In 1969, 1971 and 1973, the load line went up. Each time, she was allowed to sit deeper.
In the end, her winter freeboard, the height of her deck above the water, had shrunk from nearly fifteen feet to eleven and a half.
So she carried more, closer to the water. Nobody asked the lake.
And her deck was mostly lids. Each hatch cover weighed about fourteen thousand pounds and was held down by sixty-eight clamps, adjusted by hand.
There were no written procedures for maintaining them. Remember those clamps.
She also had no depth finder, and no way of monitoring water in her cargo hold.
If water got in down there, the first sign might be the ship itself starting to lean.
On November ninth, 1975, she finished loading in Superior, Wisconsin. Twenty-six thousand tons of iron ore pellets, bound for Detroit.
Her captain was Ernest McSorley, sixty-three years old. According to one recent book, even his rivals called him the greatest captain on the Great Lakes.
His crew of twenty-nine ranged down to Karl Peckol, a twenty-year-old watchman.
Their families were spread around Duluth, Toledo and Cleveland. Bruce Hudson, a twenty-two-year-old deckhand, was his mother's only child.
She left at about a quarter past two in the afternoon, at full speed. The gale warning came five hours later, when she was already out on the lake.
That afternoon another ore carrier had left Two Harbors, Minnesota. The Arthur M. Anderson, under Captain Jesse Bernie Cooper.
By night she was ten or twenty miles behind the Fitzgerald. Remember her too, because hers is the only account we have of how this ended.
At two in the morning, the gale warning became a storm warning.
So the two captains did the sensible thing. They left the normal shipping lanes and ran north, along the Canadian shore, to hide from the wind.
It worked for a while. Then they had to turn southeast, toward Whitefish Point and the shelter behind it, and the storm came around behind them.
At about three thirty on the afternoon of November tenth, the Fitzgerald called the Anderson.
I have a fence rail down, have lost a couple of vents, and have a list.
Cooper's crew asked if the pumps were running. Yes, both of them. And he said he would slow down, so the Anderson could close the gap.
That is a strange list of damage. A ship in a storm can lose a railing. But a list means water is somewhere it should not be.
How did it get in? And where exactly was she when it happened? Those two questions are still open.
Forty minutes later, it got worse. Both of her radars were out. She asked the Anderson to keep track of her and guide her in.
So now one ship was steering by another ship's eyes, miles away, in a snowstorm.
She tried the other way to find home. She asked the Coast Guard station at Grand Marais about the radio beacon at Whitefish Point. It was not working.
So a Swedish ship near the point, the Avafors, got a call. Its pilot later reported what he heard from the Fitzgerald's captain.
A bad list. Both radars gone. Heavy seas over the deck. He called it one of the worst seas he had ever been in.
And then a sentence that he seemed to be saying to someone beside him. Don't allow nobody on deck.
Behind her, the Anderson had her own problems. Winds of fifty-eight knots. Waves building to around twenty-five feet. At twenty past five, a sea tore away one of her lifeboats.
Later, some would describe rogue waves, groups of three. A government simulation in 2005 suggested near-hurricane winds and average waves of around twenty feet, right where she was.
Nobody on the Fitzgerald ever filed a report on that.
Just before seven, a huge sea came over the Anderson from behind and buried her deck. Captain Cooper later described what came next.
Another wave, just like the first one or bigger. She shook it off and came up. Ten miles ahead, the Fitzgerald was in the same water, with a list and no radar.
At seven o'clock the Anderson's mate told her she was ten miles ahead. Ten minutes later he called again, about another ship coming the other way.
He asked how she was doing with her problems.
The answer, as reported by the Anderson, was: We are holding our own.
That was the last anyone heard. Nobody said goodbye. Nobody knew there was anything to say.
Minutes later, the snow lifted. The men on the Anderson could suddenly see lights on the shore, twenty miles off.
The Fitzgerald should have been ten miles ahead, lit up like a small town.
There was nothing there. Not on the radar, and not out the window.
They called her again and again. Nothing. And here the paperwork enters the story.
According to Cooper's testimony, he called the Coast Guard at Soo Saint Marie, and was asked to change channels.
Then he called again, and was told to keep an eye out for a lost sixteen-foot boat.
The station's log does not mention that boat. It does record what he said over an hour after the last message.
I am very concerned with the welfare of the steamer Edmund Fitzgerald.
So who could go and look? The nearest big Coast Guard cutter was three hundred miles away. The other one was not allowed out in winds over sixty knots.
So the Coast Guard asked the only ship that had just survived it.
The Anderson had just reached Whitefish Bay. Cooper told them the seas were tremendously large, and that he would be lucky to make two or three miles an hour.
The Coast Guard left the decision to him. I'll give it a try, he said, but that's all I can do.
He turned her around and went back out. Only one other ship left the bay to join him, the William Clay Ford.
They searched for days. Ships, planes, Canadian crews, police walking the shoreline.
They found one lifeboat, half of another, two rafts and twenty-one life jackets. They found nobody.
Four days after she vanished, a Navy plane picked up a magnetic signal on the bottom.
The following May, a robot camera went down and read a name on the stern.
She lay in five hundred and thirty feet of water, about seventeen miles from Whitefish Point.
In two pieces. The bow sat upright. The stern lay upside down. And about two hundred feet of ship between them was simply wreckage on the lake floor.
A seven-hundred-foot ship does not end up like that gently. But did she break first and sink? Or sink first and break on the bottom? Everything else depends on that.
Theory one is the official one. In 1977, the Coast Guard blamed ineffective hatch covers.
In 1978, the National Transportation Safety Board called it sudden, massive flooding, from the collapse of one or more hatch covers.
Now remember the clamps. The Coast Guard concluded that few of them had been fastened.
On the wreck, the cameras studied a row of sixteen at hatch number five. Two were distorted or broken. Fourteen were undamaged, and in the open position.
Think about what that says. It says a crew sailed into November on Lake Superior without latching the lids. The deckhands one recent author interviewed say nobody does that.
And the safety board's own answer was different: the covers collapsed under the weight of the seas, latched or not.
Theory two is the shoal. North of Caribou Island, there is a patch of shallow water called Six Fathom Shoal.
The Lake Carriers' Association, which critics said was protecting its industry, argued that she scraped it, with the light and the beacon out.
And Captain Cooper testified that he and his officers watched her pass over that shallow water on radar. Three thirty, a list and lost vents, not long after.
And one member of the safety board itself agreed. Philip Hogue filed a dissent, and said he was strongly convinced she had shoaled before that three thirty call.
The chairman wrote a statement rejecting his reasoning. It is all in the same report.
Theory three is the hull. Lake waves are steep and close together, so a long ship can end up held by the bow and the stern, with nothing under the middle.
Former crewmen said she flexed in storms. In 1994, a private expedition led by Shannon spent over forty hours filming her, and concluded she broke up on the surface.
Its pictures also showed no damage to the propeller or rudder from a shoal.
Theory four is the wave. Something enormous, on top of a deck already taking water. Possible. But waves do not leave paperwork.
Each theory has people who will defend it for the rest of their lives, and each one has a hole.
The hatches do not easily explain that first call. The shoal does not show on the propeller. The hull cannot be read from a wreck that hit the bottom. And nobody measured the wave.
The author of that recent book thinks it may be a mix of them.
Here is what changed, though, whichever one is right. Depth finders became mandatory in 1977, and survival suits in 1980.
Charts of that part of the lake were improved. The 1973 load line rule was rescinded. And ships now get inspected every year, before November.
On July fourth, 1995, divers brought up the ship's bell. Forty-six relatives signed the document giving it to the museum at Whitefish Point.
In its place, they left a replica, engraved with twenty-nine names. And when the real one broke the surface, it rang.
The rest of her is still down there, and it is a grave. Captain McSorley. Karl Peckol. Bruce Hudson. All the men between them.
Bruce Hudson's mother, Ruth, had her own view of all those reports. Only thirty know, she said.
Twenty-nine men and God. And nobody's talking.
